title: Apple Explores New Vision Pro Form Factors, Sources Reveal Upcoming Design Variants
body:
Apple is reportedly developing a second generation of its Vision Pro mixed‑reality headset, and this time the company is exploring multiple form‑factors that could address the bulk and price concerns that have limited the device’s mainstream appeal. Sources familiar with the project say engineers are evaluating slimmer, lighter designs as well as a more affordable variant that could arrive within the next 12 to 18 months, signaling Apple’s intent to broaden the platform beyond early adopters and enterprise pilots.

The original Vision Pro, unveiled in early 2024, dazzled with its high‑resolution displays, advanced eye‑tracking, and a custom Apple‑silicon chip that promised unprecedented performance for immersive experiences. However, the headset’s weight—approximately 800 grams—and its $3,499 price tag sparked a wave of criticism from both consumers and industry analysts. While the device has found niche success in sectors such as design, healthcare, and education, sales volumes have fallen short of the lofty expectations set by Apple’s previous product launches. The new development effort appears aimed at overcoming those hurdles by delivering a more ergonomic and cost‑effective solution without sacrificing the core capabilities that define the Vision Pro ecosystem.

According to insiders, the design teams are prototyping two distinct directions. The first is a “compact” version that trims the headset’s bulk by re‑engineering the optics and using lighter composite materials for the frame. Early mock‑ups suggest a reduction of up to 30 percent in overall weight, bringing the device closer to the comfort levels of consumer‑grade virtual‑reality headsets currently on the market. The second approach focuses on a “budget” model that would retain the essential mixed‑reality functions but replace some of the premium components—such as the custom‑made micro‑LED displays—with more cost‑effective alternatives. This could lower the retail price to the $1,500‑$2,000 range, making the product competitive with high‑end VR headsets from rivals like Meta and Sony.

Analysts view these moves as a natural evolution for Apple’s mixed‑reality ambitions. The company’s long‑term strategy appears to hinge on creating a robust software ecosystem, anchored by visionOS, that can attract developers and content creators. A more accessible hardware platform would likely accelerate app development, expand the user base, and generate recurring revenue through the App Store and subscription services tied to immersive content. Moreover, a lighter, cheaper headset could unlock new use cases in education, remote collaboration, and consumer entertainment—areas where the current Vision Pro’s price and form factor have been prohibitive.

Supply‑chain considerations also play a role in the timing of a next‑gen device. Apple’s recent investments in advanced silicon manufacturing and its partnership with suppliers for custom optics give the company the flexibility to iterate quickly. However, scaling production of a new form factor will require retooling assembly lines and securing additional component capacity, challenges that could push the launch timeline toward the latter half of 2025. Market watchers note that Apple’s typical product cadence—introducing a refreshed version roughly every two years—fits neatly with this projected window, allowing the company to capitalize on the momentum generated by the original Vision Pro while addressing its shortcomings.

If Apple succeeds in delivering a lighter, more affordable headset, it could reshape the mixed‑reality landscape and set a new benchmark for premium immersive devices. The company’s brand cachet and integrated hardware‑software approach give it a distinct advantage over competitors that rely on third‑party ecosystems. Yet the ultimate test will be consumer adoption; even a refined design must overcome lingering skepticism about the practical utility of mixed‑reality technology in everyday life.

Looking ahead, the next iteration of Vision Pro could be the catalyst that moves mixed reality from a niche curiosity to a mainstream platform. By diversifying its hardware lineup, Apple aims to lower the entry barrier for both developers and users, fostering a virtuous cycle of content creation and consumption. If the projected timelines hold, the industry may see Apple’s mixed‑reality vision materialize in a form that feels less like a specialized instrument and more like a natural extension of personal computing—a development that could redefine how we interact with digital information in the years to come.
